newsitem.title: UK: Breakdown of major nations' offers of Zaire help.
newsitem.headline: Breakdown of major nations' offers of Zaire help.

text.p: The United Nations is close to approving an international force to open up aid routes to refugees in eastern Zaire and officials are deciding where troops would be sent and which routes they would take.
Canadian forces would lead the operation and France says it hopes the first troops will be in Zaire by the weekend.
Here is how major nations currently stand on whether to contribute troops to the multinational force:

CANADA -- says its first troops could be deployed within 48 hours of a U.N. resolution to send a multinational force. The first deployment would be a special 350-member Disaster Assistance Response Team, formed by the Canadian military to provide disaster relief at home and abroad.

FRANCE -- has spearheaded efforts to create the proposed Zaire force and says it is ready to contribute about 1,500 soldiers, 600 of them within 24 hours of receiving an international mandate to do so and a further 600 to follow 24 hours later. Paris says, however, that it will not move alone.

UNITED STATES - President Bill Clinton has tentatively agreed to order U.S. troops to join the rescue mission, expected to last about four months. Some 1,000 ground troops would be sent along with several thousand support troops on condition the mission is of limited duration and made up of a multinational force. Remembering the U.N. mission to Somalia in 1993 which led to heavy casualties among U.S. and other troops, Washington has insisted on seeing full details of the force's mandate and funding and has sent an assessment team to the region.

BELGIUM - Zaire's former colonial ruler says it is ready to send soldiers to Africa to train local troops for an eventual U.N. peacekeeping force in eastern Zaire, but says it will not take part directly in a force in Zaire, Rwanda or Burundi.

BRITAIN - says it is prepared to contribute troops to the operation but Prime Minister John Major says vital details about the mission still need to be worked out. Media reports have talked of Britain sending around 3,000 soldiers and a statement from Major's office stresses Britain would seek to maximise the safety of its troops.
GERMANY - has ruled out sending German troops to Zaire, but the government has discussed contributing financial aid.

SOUTH AFRICA - President Nelson Mandela says he is prepared in principle to contribute troops to an international force, but he wants more specific information before deciding on what size military unit to send.

SPAIN - has put troops on alert for an immediate action should the U.N. give a green light. Foreign Minister Abel Matutes says 350 to 450 Spanish soldiers would participate initially and numbers may be increased later.

THE NETHERLANDS - is expected to discuss sending troops in a parliamentary debate on Thursday about foreign and military spending. The Defence Ministry says it has begun vaccinating a company of 270 military personnel, mainly combat troops, from its Air Mobile Brigade. Any company sent to Zaire would be equipped with personal weapons plus 10 to 15 armoured personnel carriers armed with light cannon.

IRELAND - says it will provide troops for the proposed force if asked. It is expected to contribute a specialist unit of soldiers such as engineers, military police or logistics personnel. Officials say this is unlikely to exceed 100 soldiers.
FINLAND - says it will not send troops but is studying other ways it can help.
